Empirical Research Plan: “School Quality and the Black–White Earnings Gap, Southern Birth Cohorts 1920-1949”

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences-in-Differences (DDD) implemented in a stacked cohort-by-state-by-race panel.

Why DDD?  
• Two dimensions vary “naturally”: (i) race-specific school quality across Southern states, (ii) time (birth cohort).  
• Comparing (a) Black vs. White men within the same state and cohort removes state-by-cohort shocks (e.g., macro conditions).  
• Comparing across successive cohorts within the same race-state pair nets out fixed racial differences in parental background that are constant across cohorts.  
• The remaining variation is the interaction of (Race × Cohort × Quality change) – the causal effect of quality differences created by the segregated school system.

Alternative designs (IV with Rosenwald construction, RDD around Brown v. Board, etc.) are possible but require data that are not guaranteed in the current description; DDD exploits the information we know we have.

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------------
Unit of analysis: Individual i born in cohort c in state s, observed in 1970 Census.

Treatment variable  
Q_scr = race-specific school-quality of the birth cohort: we will use three continuous measures separately (pupil-teacher ratio PTR, log teacher salary SAL, and term length TERM). Each is observed at the race-state-cohort level and assigned to all individuals in that cell.

Control group / counterfactual  
Within each state–cohort cell, Whites serve as the counterfactual for Blacks; within each state–race cell, earlier cohorts serve as the counterfactual for later cohorts that enjoyed better (or worse) quality. Hence, the design is a triple difference:

(Black × Quality_scr) after differencing out  
State × Cohort FE, State × Race FE, Cohort × Race FE.

Treatment timing  
Event date = individual’s year of birth (we assign school quality prevailing when the child was age 6–17). “Pre-period” = earlier cohorts; “post-period” = later cohorts.

No running variable or cutoff (not RDD).

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel-trends in earnings between Blacks and Whites within a state would have been the same across cohorts absent changes in relative school quality.

Plausibility: During 1920-49 the South experienced few policies targeted at adult earnings that were race-specific yet systematically correlated with school-quality investments. Remaining concerns (e.g., WWII service, migration) are addressed in Section 4.

A2. Exogeneity of within-state, within-race, across-cohort changes in school inputs to unobserved cohort-specific shocks in labor-market productivity.

Plausibility: School budgets were set by county/state legislatures often for reasons (cotton‐tax receipts, political shifts) unrelated to future national labor markets; we will implement state-specific cohort linear trends and lagged economic controls to bolster credibility.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-race spillovers in quality inputs).

Plausibility: In the segregated South Black and White school systems were largely separate; still, small spillovers through overall district funding could exist but work against finding a strong effect (attenuation bias).

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Selective Out-Migration  
If higher-quality cohorts are more likely to move to high-wage Northern states, observed earnings reflect migration not schooling.

Mitigation:  
• Use place-of-birth × place-of-residence information to code migrants; run baseline on “stayers” (born and residing in South).  
• Include “migrant” dummy interacted with race to allow differential returns.  
• Show results robust to inverse-probability weighting that re-weights stayers to match out-migration propensities.

T2. Concurrent Changes in Returns-to-Education (e.g., Civil Rights Act)  
Black cohorts entering the labor market in the 1960s benefited from anti-discrimination laws.

Mitigation:  
• Include cohort-by-race fixed effects that soak up anything common to all Blacks of a cohort regardless of state quality.  
• Add linear (and quadratic) interactions Race × (birth year) to capture national time trends.  
• Conduct placebo using Whites only: regress their earnings on the Black quality series; coefficient should be zero.

T3. Measurement Error in Historical Quality Data  
Aggregated records may be noisy, attenuating coefficients.

Mitigation:  
• Use multiple indicators (PTR, SAL, TERM) and estimate a latent-quality principal-component index.  
• Instrument each noisy measure with the other two (errors orthogonal) – an IV-errors-in-variables approach (Hausman et al., 1998).  
• Cluster standard errors two-ways (state, cohort) to reflect sampling error in quality aggregates.

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------
library(data.table)  # fast manipulation
library(fixest)      # high-dim FE regressions
library(readr)
library(sandwich)    # robust VCOV
library(modelsummary)

# ---------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# ---------------------------------------------
census  <- fread("census_1970_individual.csv")   # id, state_birth, cohort, race, earnings70, migrant
quality <- fread("school_quality_state_race_cohort.csv") # state_birth, cohort, race, ptr, ln_sal, term

# ---------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge and construct variables
# ---------------------------------------------
setkeyv(census,  c("state_birth","cohort","race"))
setkeyv(quality, c("state_birth","cohort","race"))
df <- quality[census]  # left join

# Create indicators
df[, black := as.integer(race == "Black")]
df[, ln_earn := log(earnings70)]

# Optional composite index
df[, z_ptr  := scale(ptr)]
df[, z_sal  := scale(ln_sal)]
df[, z_term := scale(term)]
df[, qual_pc1 := prcomp(~z_ptr + z_sal + z_term, .SD)$x[,1], .SDcols=c("z_ptr","z_sal","z_term")]

# ---------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DDD regression
# ln(earnings) = β * (Quality × Black) + γ Quality + δ Black + FE + ε
# FE: state*cohort, state*race, cohort*race
# ---------------------------------------------
est_main <- feols(ln_earn ~ black*ptr + black*ln_sal + black*term |
                    state_birth^cohort + state_birth^black + cohort^black,
                  data = df, cluster = ~state_birth + cohort)

etable(est_main)

# ---------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness check 1: migrants removed
# ---------------------------------------------
est_stayers <- feols(ln_earn ~ black*ptr + black*ln_sal + black*term |
                       state_birth^cohort + state_birth^black + cohort^black,
                     data = df[migrant == 0],
                     cluster = ~state_birth + cohort)
etable(est_main, est_stayers)

# ---------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness check 2: placebo on Whites
# Should be ≈0 if design is valid
# ---------------------------------------------
est_white_placebo <- feols(ln_earn ~ ptr + ln_sal + term |
                             state_birth^cohort,
                           data = df[black == 0],
                           cluster = ~state_birth + cohort)
summary(est_white_placebo)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition and extant literature (e.g., Card & Krueger 1992) suggest that:
• Lower pupil–teacher ratios, higher teacher salaries, and longer terms raise adult earnings.  
• Because Black schools started with worse quality, marginal improvements should have higher returns for Blacks, narrowing the Black–White gap.

Approximate magnitude: a one-student reduction in the PTR (≈10 percentile improvement) is expected to raise Black men’s log earnings by 1.5–2 percent (~$600–$800 in 1970 dollars), roughly half the elasticities reported in contemporary studies.

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DDD)
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable/absent)
------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Correct temporal ordering (quality measured before earnings) ………………… 1  
C2: Parallel trends (plausibility + visual evidence) ……………………………………… 0.8  
C3: No differential composition changes (migration, mortality) …………………… 0.6  
C4: No simultaneous interventions correlated with treatment ……………………… 0.7  
C5: Accurate measurement of treatment and outcome ……………………………… 0.7  

Average = 0.76 → design is reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.

------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
